2. While issuing Rule a direction was given to maintain status-quo with regard to the custody of the victim girl and the case in the court below was allowed to proceed as usual. Subsequently on 3.4.91 on the prayer made on behalf of the petitioner, the opposite parties No.2 to 5 (accused in the case out of which the present Rule arises) as mentioned in paragraph 2(ii) of the application for amendment, were impleaded as parties and Rule was also issued against them. Simultaneously prayer for conversion of the application under section 491 CrPC to an application under section 439 read with section 435 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was also made. As no order for conversion as prayed for was passed earlier, Mr. Ruhul Amin II, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner prayed for passing an order allowing him to make necessary amendment sought for in the application and accordingly the prayer was allowed on 22.1.92, being not opposed by the learned Advocate appearing 'for the opposite parties. 

 3. In the application filed by the petitioner before this court, the petitioner being the father of the victim girl made grievance against the order dated 17.10.90 passed by the Sessions Judge Noakhali in Criminal Miscellaneous Case 1041 of 1990 and 1064 of 1990 by which the order passed by the learned Upazila Magistrate on 10.9.90 in GR Case No. 114 of 1990 under section 366A of the renal Code read with section 4(b) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 passed' by the learned Upazila Magistrate, Sadar, Noakhali, was affirmed. 

 4. The facts of the case, briefly stated, are as follows: 

 Md. Ashrafuddin, son of the petitioner lodged an FIR at the Sudharam Police Station on 19.8.90 stating that Kazi Rehana Akhter alias Lipi, the daughter of the petitioner aged 14 years, while a student of class IX of Maijdee Balika Biddyaniketon left home for school at 10-00 AM on 15.8.90 as usual along with the main road and while she reached at a point near ''Napiterpole' accused Fakhrul Islam alias Litan, Faruq and Shahnewaz forcibly kidnapped her on the point of arms and lifted her to the house of accused Faruq in a rickshaw. On her raising hue and cry accused Fakhrul Islam pressed her mouth by handkerchief. Getting information accused Din Islam Nur Islam, Shamsul Islam alias Swapan, Mamun and Mintoo went to the house and after having consultations removed Kazi Rehana Akhter to the residence of one Rashid at Chittagong. The petitioner and his sons and others searched for her at different places for 2 days and having failed to trace out her the son of the petitioner made a GD Entry in the local police station. It came to be known that accused Faruq had complicity in the matter and he disclosed to the police on interrogation that accused Fakhrul Islam and Shahnewaz kidnapped her and confined her at the residence; of accused Rashid. From Chittagong the accused removed her to Eklashpur village in Noakhali at the house of his Fufu. The police registered a case being Sudharam PS Case No. 9(8)90 under section 366A of the Penal Code (GR Case No. 114 of 1990). 

 6. The learned Magistrate after hearing the matter by his order dated 12.9.90 found that the victim girl being a minor and incapable of exercising her free will would go to the custody of her father, in default, she would remain in judicial custody. Accused Fakhrul Islam alias Liton was, however, granted bail. The accused party moved the Sessions Judge in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 1041 of 1990 seeking the release of the victim girl and the petitioner also filed criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 1064 of 1990 seeking the custody of the minor girl. Both the applications were heard together and the learned Sessions Judge was of the view that the victim girl; would be hardly 15 years and observed that she was not entitled to exercise her option and as such she would go to the custody of father in default she would remain in the judicial custody. Thereafter the police submitted charge sheet on 14.11.90 in the case under section 366A of the Penal, Code and section 4(b) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983. 

 9. Mr. Md. Abdur Rashid, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 2 raised a preliminary objection as to the maintainability of the application under section 439 read with section 435 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as it stands now after its conversion from an application under section 491 CrPC on the prayer of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. The learned Advocate submits that the application filed before the Sessions Judge against the order of the learned Magistrate was practically an application under section 439A CrPC and the said application having been finally disposed of by the learned Sessions Judge, no application by way of second revision against the final order of the Sessions Judge could be entertained by this court. The learned Advocate relied on the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 127. In reply, Mr. Ruhul Amin submits that the application filed before the Sessions Judge by the father of the girl seeking custody of his minor daughter was not an application under section 439A CrPC but it was in the nature of a miscellaneous case and as such was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 1064 of 1990 and was heard along with the bail application filed on behalf of the accused being Miscellaneous Case No. 1041 of 1990 and, therefore, the application under section 439 CrPC filed before this court against the order of the Sessions Judge passed in those Miscellaneous Cases is quite competent. From the record it appears that the application on which the order was passed was not made and for that matter was not registered as an application under section 439A CrPC and the said order having not been passed by the learned Sessions Judge in exercise of his power vested under section 439A, the present application does not fall in the category of second revision and, therefore, the question of maintainability is answered in favour of the petitioner. 

 12. Thus in order to constitute an offence under section 361 BPC the allegations relate to taking away of a person, if a male must be under the age of 14 years, and if a female under the age of 16 years, out of the lawful guardianship of the person having the custody but for the purpose of Constituting an offence of abduction bringing it under the definition of section 362 of the Penal Code or within the ambit of section 366A, the age of the girl is stated to be below 18 years which section does not speak of taking away from lawful guardianship. In the instant case out of which the present Rule arises, the age of the victim girl has been shown below 16 years and it is alleged that she has been kidnapped from her lawful guardianship. But the case has been started under section 366A of the Penal Code and the charge sheet has also been submitted under the said section of the Penal Code. If the girl is found to be below 16 years the taking away out of the keeping of the lawful guardian constitute an offence, but if the girl is found to be of the age of 16 years or over she cannot be said to be a minor within the meaning of section 361 punishable under section 366 of the Penal Code. The above is the finding in the case of Fatema Begum alias Urmila Rani Vs. Gageswar Nath and the Sate reported in 9 BLD (1989) 469. Though it does not constitute an offence of kidnapping under section 363 and if the girl is found to have been aged 16 years or above, nevertheless it remains an offence of abduction under section 366 and or under section 366A of the Penal Code, if the girl found to have been taken away is below the age of 18 years. Thus we find that for the purpose of determining the minority so far it relates to section 361 the age of the victim girl is to be below 16 years and if that be so, the question of commission of offence for taking away the girl from the lawful guardianship will arise. If the age of the girl is 18 years or above no question of getting the custody of the victim girl arises. If the age of the subject is found below 16 years the father is unquestionably the guardian of the minor girl according to the Majority Act as well as under the provision of law as defined under section 361 of the Penal Code. This is the settled law of the land. But there is a great controversy over the question upto what age a girl is to be considered minor. The moot question which has been raised in the case by the learned Advocate of the respective parties is whether a girl on attaining the age of 16 years becomes sui juris for the purpose of exercising her free will to marry anybody of her choice or to remain under the guardianship of the father till she attains the age of 18 years according to the Majority Act. From the materials placed by both the parties and the look of the girl and the maturity of understanding it appears that the girl is aged at present over 16 years. As the actual age cannot be ascertained at this stage without entering into the evidence both, oral and documentary, it should be left for the trial Court to decide. If it is found that the girl is aged less than 16 years as submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, the father is, of course, the best well-wisher and he is entitled to the custody of her daughter under the Majority Act and Guardians and Wards Act. If it is assumed for the sake of argument that the girl is aged 16 years or above but below 18 years in that case also Mr. Ruhul Amin submits that she is treated to be a minor under the Guardians and Wards Act and for that matter the father is entitled to the custody of the victim girl. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the petitioner referred to and relied on the case of Sukhendra Chandra Das Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs reported in 42 DLR 79, (Rele 85) the views taken in the said decision are as follows: 

 13. Next cited case in this regard is the case of Prafulla Kumar Bhattacharya Vs. Ministry of Home Affairs Govt. of Bangladesh reported in 28 DLR (HC) 123. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has also relied on the decision of the case of Krishna Pada Dutta Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh reported in 42 DLR 297 (Para 15) wherein it is Held: 

 "In the absence of a neutral home in our country for unfortunate allegedly kidnapped immature girls, the moot point in this case for determination is the age of the girl, that is, whether the girl is sui juris (a person having full legal capacity to act) or not on the facts alleged and proof furnished. Because in essence it is a case for custody of the girl Shukla Rani Datta and hence her majority or minority will be the deciding factor to allow her to go wherever she likes or to give her to the custody of her lawful guardian." 

 14. While arguing the case the learned Advocate for the petitioner also referred to the judgment of the case Sumati Begum Vs. Refique Ullah and another delivered in Criminal Revision No. 170/ 1990 (Dhaka). In the said case after elaborate discussion with regard to the provision of law and the principle laid down in different cases the learned court observed: 

 15. Regarding the custody of girl Mr. Md. Abdur Rashid has cited the case of Jahanara Begum alias Jotsna Rani Saha Vs. State and another reported in 15 DLR 148, wherein Sattar J speaking for the court held: 

 16. In the above cited case the learned Judges held that it will not be proper to place the girl under custody against her will particularly when she was witness in the charge sheet. Though in the first information report the age of the girl was stated to be 14 years and the girl stated her age as 18 years, in the case of Kiran Bala Chowdhury Vs. The State reported in 17 DLR 544 it is observed that: 

 "The age of the girl is a material point to be determined at the trial, if any, under section 366 of the Penal Code on evidence that may be laid down in the case. It is further observed that the detention of Rani Bala is illegal, For the Superintendent of the Dacca Central Jail to throw out a minor girl in the street on her release will be an act of irresponsibility which he cannot be permitted to do." 

 17. In the case of Prafulla Kumar Bhattacharya Vs. Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh reported in 28 DLR 123, it is held: 

 "For, if the girl is minor the person best entitled to her custody will be her father, the petitioner. But the interest of the girl herself will also be taken into consideration in the light of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890. On the other hand, if the girl is major, being aged 16 years or over, her will, in the circumstances disclosed above, must prevail and since she is not an accused in the Police Case as referred to, she cannot be detained against her will." 

 18. The above view was taken in line with the decisions taken by our court in the case reported in 8 DLR 293 and 15 DLR 148. Next case cited By Mr. Rashid is the case of Mushtaq Ahmed Vs. Mirza Muhammad Amin and another reported in 1962 PLD (Karachi) 442 wherein it is held: 

 "According to Muslim Law the minority of a male or female terminates when he or she attains puberty. Puberty is presumed on the completion of the 15th year according to the law by which the parties are governed. Under the Majority Act of 181, 5 minority ceases on the completion of the 18th year. Section 2 of the said Act, however, 'makes an exception in matters relating to marriage, dower, divorce and adoption. Thus for the purposes of the marriage the rule of Muhammadan Law must apply in this case, according to which any person who has attained puberty is entitled to act in the matter of marriage on attaining the age of 15 years. Reference may be made to para 348 of Mulla's Muhammadan Law, 15th Edition page 290. It is true that a female under 16 years of age comes within the definition of child and a male of above 18 years of age who contracts a child marriage is liable to be punished, but there is nothing in the Child Marriage Restraint Act which affects the validity of such a marriage. The validity of the marriage in the present case must be determined according to the rule of Muhammadan Law and according to that law that marriage is valid as Mst. Shogufta Parveen, even according to her father, was more than 15 years of age on the date of marriage and must be presumed to have attained puberty. The Child Marriage Restraint Act merely punishes the male for contracting a marriage with a child but it does not render the marriage invalid." 

 19. Oldfield J in the case of Muthu Ibrahim and three others reported in 37 (1914) ILR (Mad) 567 held: 

 20. In the case of Ananda Mohan Banerjee Vs. State and others reported in DLR 315 the girl's father by filing an application under section 491 CrPC prayed that the girl should be restored to him he being the lawful guardian of the minor girl. On the  other hand, it was 'contended that the' girl was aged over 16 years and as such there cannot be any offence of kidnapping under section 366 of the Penal Code and she cannot be forced into the custody of her parents against her wishes. It was held that the question of custody loses its relevance when the girl concerned is found to be aged over 16.years. She neither being an accused nor a witness in the case cannot be held in detention under court's order but is free to go to any place of her liking. In taking this view relevant case reported in 15 DLR 148, wherein it was held that the girl who is found to be over 16 years cannot be kept in custody against her will was relied on. In the case of Zafar Khan Vs. Muhammad Ashraf Bhatti reported in PLD 1975 (Lahore) 234 the case of Bindu Vs. Mst. Bugli reported in 73 PR 1909 has been referred to. In the said case Rottingham and Shah Din JJ. observed: 

 21. In the case of Zafar Khan Vs. Muhammad Ashraf Bhatti reported in PLD 1975 (Lahore) 234 the case of Bindu vs.  Mst. Bugli reported in 73 PR 1909 has been referred to. In the said case Rottingham and Shah Din JJ. observed: 

 22. The same view was taken in the case reported in AIR 1932 (Kah) 280, AIR 1938 Cal. 71, PLD 1949 Lah 75 wherein it was held that marriage under Muslim Law is in the nature of a contract and as such requires the free and unfettered consent of the parties to it. 

 23. Thus, for the purpose of custody of the girl age of majority laid down in the Majority Act, 1975 with Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 the age of 18 years is a factor for determining as to whether the girl is major or she is to be given to the custody of the guardian. It is needless to state that reference of the age of sixteen in case of a female minor in section 361 of the Penal Code is only for the purpose of commission of the' offence punishable under section 366 of the Penal Code and not for the purpose of deciding whether she is sui juris. 

 24. In the instant case the girl eloped with the accused Fakhrul Islam alias Liton on 15.8.90 and is stated to have married him. If it is found that the girl was below 16 years while she was taken away by any person from the lawful guardianship of the father without his consent he would be guilty of kidnapping and the consent of the girl and the intention of the accused will have no relevancy. The, question will arise whether taking away from the guardianship of father will constitute an offence under section 363 Penal Code; if 'the girl is found to be 16 years or above. The section itself postulates and the series of judicial pronouncements have taken the view that there will be no offence under section 363, if the girl was 16 or over as for the purpose of constituting an offence of kidnapping the girl must be below the age of 16 years and if it is found that the girl has attained  the age of 16 years or over for the purpose of criminal case the father loses the right of custody of his daughter particularly-when she is said to have married out of her free will. In the instant case at the time-of alleged occurrence the age of the girl was shown as 13 years 3 months 13 days on the averments of the father that she was born on 1st July, 1977. In support of which the school transfer certificate was produced from the side of the father and a report of the Medical Board shows that she was aged 15 years at the relevant dale when she was medically examined. The girl in her statement under section 164 CrPC stated that she was over 18 years and the certificate issued by the Headmaster Sonagazi Primary School was produced on behalf of the accused showing her date of birth as on 1st July, 1972. So according to the version of the petitioner the girl was below 16 years at the relevant time and according to the opposite parties she was above 18 years. There is a dispute as to whether the victim girl attained the age of 16 years or not on the date of occurrence which can only be determined on evidence at the time of trial, both oral and documentary and on determination of the age of the victim girl it could be decided whether any offence under section 363 of the Penal Code is committed or not But for the purpose of determining whether the prayer of the father for taking the custody of the girl. he allowed or not a prima facie view can be taken on the basis of the averments made and documents produced by both the parties, The girl was medically examined on 26.8.90 and according to the medical report she was about 15 years on that day. On the very face of it inference can be drawn that she is over 16 years now. The victim girl herself made statement before the Magistrate under section 164 wherein she claimed to have attained the age of 18 years. The certificate issued by the Headmaster Sonagazi Primary School on 11.9.90 also shows that she is over 16 years, though the said certificate has been challenged by the petitioner. As there is controversy and dispute over the age of the girl vis-a-vis the claim of custody made by the father on our order the girl was produced in the Court's chamber and we had the occasion to see her asking her a few questions for testing her maturity of understanding. It seemed to us that the girl is mature intelligent and sharp and has got sufficient knowledge and understanding of the realities of life. She stated that she voluntarily left her father's house at the time while she was major and she married Liton on her free will and lived together for some time having sexual relationship with him which also gets support from the medical report. The girl claimed herself to be major and stated that she voluntarily married Liton with whom she had love affairs from some time before the alleged date of occurrence. She also expressed her determined unwillingness to go to the custody of her father and preferred to remain under the judicial custody. From the oral examination of the girl and from her demean our and our knowledge and experience about the human conduct we find sufficient reasons to hold that she is not less than 16 years now though the question of determination of her proper age is left for the trial Court to decide on evidence. Whatever observation we have made with regard to the age of the girl is based on our impression and inference only for the purpose of her custody. Now the question arises if the girl is of 16 years or over whether she should be forced to go to the custody of the father as prayed for by him. In 15 DLR Case it has been found that the girl or the age of 16 years or over cannot be detained against her will. In the instant case she is in judicial custody but not against her will but to compel her to go to custody of the father appears to us to be against her will expressed before us which may amount to mental torture. In the instant case it appears that the girl also has entered into the contract of marriage of course it is to be seen whether the girl was a willing party and gave her free consent as she now says. If it is found so, then the marriage will be valid. Under Muslim Law, puberty of girl is presumed at age of 15 years and on 'attaining that age she can validly enter into contract of marriage. 

 27. In the present case there is a controversy with regard to the age of victim girl from whose appearance and conduct it appears that she is aged 16 years or above and is quite mature in understanding. As she is an unwilling person she cannot be forced to go to her father which may cause mental pressure to her and prejudice to the accused persons who are facing trial. Under such circumstances, it is always safe to keep the victim girl isolated from any influence which may be necessitated to ensure justice and fair play. A girl has been kept now in judicial custody on the order of the Magistrate though she is neither an accused nor a witness in the case. The custody or detention of a victim girl is of much difference from the custody of the alleged criminal and political detenu. Such judicial custody has the complexion of the custody of a guardian. This custody is necessary for giving a chance to the girl to make up her mind and to develop her independent opinion free from external influence and pressure. The facts and circumstances of each case will determine as to how and when the inherent discretion of the court is to be exercised. The principle laid down is that the girl over the age of 16 years should not be given to and kept in custody against her will. But in the instant case it appears that the girl is not unwilling to remain in the judicial custody but she is most unwilling to go to the custody of her father. In such cases it will be worthwhile to make observation that the neutral homes are the best places for keeping the victim girl segregated for a temporary period and in the absence of such neutral homes complicated question will arise as to whether a girl, who is neither a witness nor an accused, should be kept in jail and whether the girl could be released on bail, if prayed for. We feel that it is necessary to set up neutral homes where the minor girls becoming victims of such circumstances could be kept temporarily away from the criminals and in the custody and care of responsible persons so as to exclude the possibility of any external influence. In the instant case on the prayer made by the father for the custody of the victim girl the Magistrate passed the order that the victim girl could be released and given to the custody of the father, in the alternative she will remain in the judicial custody. On being aggrieved, the father filed application before the Sessions Judge which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 1064 of 1990 and the learned Sessions Judge after hearing the learned Advocate and on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case affirmed the order of the Magistrate with the finding that the victim girl Rehana Akhtar alias Lipi may go with her father, or in the alternative shall remain in judicial custody. We also find that the learned Courts below were quite justified in passing such order. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has made grievance against the order stating that the alternative direction has practically rendered ineffective the first part of the order which entitles the father to get the custody of the daughter. We have already found that giving the girl to the custody of the father against her will if she has attained the age of 16 years now having also attained maturity of understanding may cause prejudice to her and to the accused persons in the case. Under such circumstances she could be allowed to go anywhere exercising her free will but that course would have the effect of throwing her out from the judicial custody to the street. Instead, the learned courts below having taken into consideration all the aspects of the case passed the order for keeping her in judicial custody, in case she is not willing to go with her father and the said order, we think, has been passed taking the most rational view of the matter by the courts below and we do not find any illegality or impropriety in the order of the Sessions Judge allowing the victim girl to go with her father, or in the alternative to remain in the judicial custody and accordingly we hold that the order does not call for any interference. Before parting with the case, let us not be understood to have expressed ourselves taking any decision with regard to the age of the victim girl and whatever view we have expressed has been taken only for the limited purpose of the prayer for the custody of the girl at this stage. The trial Court will, however, be at liberty to decide the point relating to the age of the victim girl in connection with the criminal case on evidence to be adduced by the parties. 

 28. Under the facts and circumstances of the case we again reiterate that the girl if so wishes will go to the custody of the father or in the alternative she will remain in the judicial custody till the disposal of the criminal case which may be taken up for disposal with utmost expedition, preferably within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of the order. If for any reason whatsoever the criminal case takes a longer time for its disposal the victim girl will have the option to move the original court for her own release, if so advised and the courts below will be at liberty to pass appropriate order as they deem fit and proper on hearing all the parties concerned in the case.
